trial.ground_truth: Catalog reads bypass cache and invalidate catalog key
trial.predicted_root_cause: inventory-service's /products cache has been neutralized: the Redis catalog key does not exist (catalog_ttl = -2, i.e. key with no TTL / never set), and the read path itself deletes it. Traces show each GET /products executes EXISTS, GET (miss), then DEL against Redis before falling through to Postgres `SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 40`. Because the key is deleted on every read (or never repopulated), 100% of requests hit the database. This raised inventory-service db_qps from a ~0.16 baseline to ~7.4 rps — a ~45x amplification — visible both in Prometheus db_qps windows and in pg_stat_statements call deltas for the product query. HTTP latency remained low (~4ms) and errors 0, so this is a cache-effectiveness/invalidation regression producing DB amplification and pool pressure, not a latency or availability outage.

regression_risks: Recommended SET ... EX 30 introduces a TTL-based invalidation window; if a writer also invalidates, stale stock/price may be served for up to 30s — a correctness regression for inventory data.
Removing a DEL could reintroduce a stale-cache path on stock mutations; the suggested fix does not specify writer-side invalidation coordination.
Recommended alerts on db_qps/hit-ratio may be noisy because existing Redis counters mix control-plane and business traffic (per bundle note), risking false positives.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Insufficient for the specific mechanism. No test or trace excerpt shows the DEL-on-read sequence; no code path for the /products cache handler is in scope (only generic redis helper). TTL=-2 snapshots plus moving-call deltas support 'cache ineffective', but do not isolate read-path eviction from writer omission. The observed catalog_ttl -2→5 transition is an operator restoration, not an AI-patched fix, and was not re-measured with db_qps/hit-ratio to confirm return to the ~0.16 baseline.

Core claim "inventory-service /products catalog Redis key is absent (catalog_ttl=-2), so reads fall through to Postgres, amplifying DB calls" is well supported: three independent redis snapshots show catalog_ttl=-2 (E-b52641fbe43f4a9c, E-7a8b2ac555b840be, E-a385827834dd4076); pg_stat_statements shows the exact products LIMIT $1 query with growing calls (E-524c19bb8fd8494a delta +8; E-57d27c4f4c3c4ca3; before/after statements calls 2378→2423) and idle inventory-service connections holding it; and db_pool shows pool_available=4/requests_waiting=0 with low ~4ms latency (E-64ebd526b46e4d07, E-4775d38c0c124f36), consistent with amplification-not-outage.

decision.root_cause: inventory-service's /products cache has been neutralized: the Redis catalog key does not exist (catalog_ttl = -2, i.e. key with no TTL / never set), and the read path itself deletes it. Traces show each GET /products executes EXISTS, GET (miss), then DEL against Redis before falling through to Postgres `SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 40`. Because the key is deleted on every read (or never repopulated), 100% of requests hit the database. This raised inventory-service db_qps from a ~0.16 baseline to ~7.4 rps — a ~45x amplification — visible both in Prometheus db_qps windows and in pg_stat_statements call deltas for the product query. HTTP latency remained low (~4ms) and errors 0, so this is a cache-effectiveness/invalidation regression producing DB amplification and pool pressure, not a latency or availability outage.
llm_findings: Trace E-3f4e7f1510ec483d shows inventory-service GET /products issuing EXISTS + GET to Redis then a DEL to the same keyspace before calling Postgres — the read path destroys its own cache entry.
catalog_ttl=-2 on two independent Redis snapshots (E-b52641fbe43f4a9c, E-7a8b2ac555b840be): the catalog key has no TTL because it is not present.
inventory db_qps scaled ~45x (0.164 → 7.44) with flat request_rps ~7.6, so per-request DB calls rose, indicating cache bypass (E-54a93a3eeb6e4cef).
pg_stat_statements call_delta +8/+6 on `SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT $1` and mean_exec_time ~0.11ms rule out slow SQL (E-524c19bb8fd8494a, E-57d27c4f4c3c4ca3).
inventory pool healthy after amplification: requests_waiting=0, pool_available=4, requests_errors=16/54367 — DB amplification, not pool exhaustion (E-64ebd526b46e4d07).
Kafka lag 0 (E-fd0af47d8623493f, E-4c19fce866154d62) and flat gateway/order/payment latencies indicate this is a cache-effectiveness defect, not an availability outage.
decision.recommended_fix: 1) Inspect the inventory-service /products cache handler and remove the DEL/setex-invalidation call executing on the read path; the read should GET and, on miss, SET the catalog key with a positive TTL (e.g. SET catalog:products EX 30) rather than delete it. 2) Verify the writer/replenisher actually sets the key with expiry — catalog_ttl=-2 shows it is never created. 3) Add a cache hit-ratio alert scoped to inventory-service product keys (excluding control-plane traffic) plus an alert on inventory db_qps vs request rate to catch this amplification class. 4) Re-run after fix and confirm catalog_ttl is > 0 and inventory db_qps returns near the 0.16 baseline while /products latency stays flat.
decision.reasoning_summary: Two independent sources corroborate: (1) Redis shows catalog_ttl=-2 on two separate snapshots (E-b52641fbe43f4a9c, E-7a8b2ac555b840be), meaning the catalog/product key is absent or TTL-less; (2) Prometheus measured db_qps for inventory-service rising 0.60→3.36→7.44 across the window versus a 0.164 baseline, while request_rps stayed flat at ~7.6 (E-54a93a3eeb6e4cef), proving DB calls per request increased rather than traffic. The trace E-3f4e7f1510ec483d shows inventory-service's GET /products span (processID p1) issuing an EXISTS and GET to redis followed by a DEL and falling through to Postgres, confirming the read path evicts the very key it should populate. pg_stat_statements call deltas +8 and +6 on the products LIMIT $1 query (E-524c19bb8fd8494a, E-57d27c4f4c3c4ca3) and multiple inventory-service connections holding that same statement confirm the downstream effect. No slow query (mean_exec_time ~0.11ms), no errors, no pool queueing (requests_waiting=0, pool_available=4 in E-64ebd526b46e4d07), so DB amplification is the mechanism, not the consequence. The cache handler itself is outside the allowlisted source scope so a code patch is not appropriate; remediation is operational.

deterministic_signals.explanation: Catalog TTL=-2 reproduced on two snapshots; the /products trace shows GET miss then DEL to redis followed by a product SELECT in Postgres, and product-query call_delta rose while inventory db_qps climbed ~45x over baseline. Cache effectiveness is indeed degraded by a read-path eviction/no-write, not by Redis connection contention.

remaining_uncertainty: The exact source of the DEL on the read path is not visible in the allowlisted scope (services/runtime.py, services/pricing.py, tests/pricing_contract.py); the inventory product-cache handler file was not accessible.
Redis keyspace_hits/misses counters are cumulative and include control-plane traffic, so they corroborate but do not quantify the inventory-specific hit ratio.
It is not certain whether the key is never written (writer bug) in addition to being deleted on read; TTL=-2 is consistent with both.

regression_risks: Recommended SET ... EX 30 introduces a TTL-based invalidation window; if a writer also invalidates, stale stock/price may be served for up to 30s — a correctness regression for inventory data.
Removing a DEL could reintroduce a stale-cache path on stock mutations; the suggested fix does not specify writer-side invalidation coordination.
Recommended alerts on db_qps/hit-ratio may be noisy because existing Redis counters mix control-plane and business traffic (per bundle note), risking false positives.
critic.test_sufficiency: Insufficient for the specific mechanism. No test or trace excerpt shows the DEL-on-read sequence; no code path for the /products cache handler is in scope (only generic redis helper). TTL=-2 snapshots plus moving-call deltas support 'cache ineffective', but do not isolate read-path eviction from writer omission. The observed catalog_ttl -2→5 transition is an operator restoration, not an AI-patched fix, and was not re-measured with db_qps/hit-ratio to confirm return to the ~0.16 baseline.
critic.verification_summary:
Core claim "inventory-service /products catalog Redis key is absent (catalog_ttl=-2), so reads fall through to Postgres, amplifying DB calls" is well supported: three independent redis snapshots show catalog_ttl=-2 (E-b52641fbe43f4a9c, E-7a8b2ac555b840be, E-a385827834dd4076); pg_stat_statements shows the exact products LIMIT $1 query with growing calls (E-524c19bb8fd8494a delta +8; E-57d27c4f4c3c4ca3; before/after statements calls 2378→2423) and idle inventory-service connections holding it; and db_pool shows pool_available=4/requests_waiting=0 with low ~4ms latency (E-64ebd526b46e4d07, E-4775d38c0c124f36), consistent with amplification-not-outage.

However, the strongest mechanistic claim — "the read path itself DELs the key" — is NOT directly evidenced. E-3f4e7f1510ec483d's preview only shows the server span GET /products (9453us); no EXISTS/GET/DEL redis child spans are visible in the supplied excerpt, and trace E-4b64564d05f24115 only shows a "GET /products http send" internal span. The cited code (E-94e3304a6e07400c, E-f577eb2fac2945a0) contains no /products cache handler — only a generic `fault()` EXISTS helper on 'fault:*-' keys. So "DEL on read path" is plausible but unconfirmed, and the same TTL=-2 is equally consistent with a never-written/writer-side bug. Crucially, ttl<0 is not proof of deletion semantics.

Furthermore, the NO_CODE_PATCH decision means no fix was applied and the only measured before/after is an operator restoration (catalog_ttl -2 → 5 in E-270c8db057d54cdb) with 20s windows, flat 7.6 rps and unchanged ~3-5ms latency — observational corroboration, not a controlled proof of unique mechanism, as the bundle's causality_limit itself states. Category CACHE_MISS diagnosis is defensible; the specific "read-path eviction regression" mechanism is under-evidenced.
